title: Signs of a Failing Shower Pan & Hidden Damage Under Tile | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: How to recognize a failing shower pan, what happens under the tile before you see it, and how to tell a leaking pan from a leaking drain or grout.
h1: The Signs of a Failing Shower Pan, and the Damage Happening Under the Tile
intro: You have probably been noticing it for a while without deciding it was a problem. A patch of baseboard in the hallway that stays a shade darker than the rest. A grout line that keeps going soft no matter how many times you re-caulk it. A smell in the bathroom that comes back a day after you clean. None of it is dramatic enough to call anyone about, so it sits there, and you walk past it, and some part of you keeps filing it under things to look at later. That gap between knowing something is wrong and being able to name what it is can be its own kind of weight. It is not carelessness. A shower pan fails quietly and slowly, in a place nobody can see, and the house gives you only small hints for a long time before it gives you a clear one.

sections.heading: A shower pan is a waterproof basin, not the tile
sections.body:
The tile and grout on your shower floor are not what keeps water out of your house. Grout is porous by design. Water passes through it, and it always has. Underneath sits the real barrier: a shower pan. In older homes that may be a hot-mopped layer of asphalt-saturated felt, or a sheet of PVC or CPE membrane folded up the walls a few inches and clamped into a two-part drain assembly. In newer builds it is often a foam preformed pan or a liquid-applied membrane rolled over the substrate. Whichever it is, the pan slopes toward the drain and carries the water that made it through the grout back into the weep holes at the base of the drain flange.

So a failing shower pan is not usually a hole you can see. It is a membrane that has cracked at a fold, a drain clamp that has loosened, weep holes packed solid with thinset or mineral scale, or a corner where the membrane was cut short during the original install. The tile above can look perfect for years while the water underneath goes somewhere it was never meant to go.

sections.heading: The signs, roughly in the order homeowners notice them
sections.body: Most of these show up outside the shower, not inside it, which is exactly why they are easy to misread.

cards.heading: Loose, hollow, or cracking floor tile
cards.body: Tap the shower floor with a knuckle or the handle of a screwdriver. A tile bedded in sound mortar sounds solid and dull. A tile over a saturated, degraded bed sounds hollow and slightly higher pitched. Cracks that reopen after repair, or a tile that flexes underfoot, usually mean the material below has broken down from constant moisture rather than the tile being defective.

cards.heading: Grout and caulk that will not stay put
cards.body: If you have recaulked the same corner three times and it keeps darkening, softening, or pulling away, the joint is not the problem. Movement or trapped water behind it is. Grout that stays wet-looking hours after the last shower, or that crumbles to powder when you scrape it, is a symptom, not a cause.

cards.heading: Damage on the other side of the wall
cards.body: Walk the room behind or beside the shower. Look at the bottom four to six inches of the baseboard, the edge of the door casing, and the flooring seam nearest the wet wall. Cupped or peeling laminate, stained or swollen baseboard, lifting vinyl edges, and paint that blisters low on the wall are all classic signs that water is exiting the shower at floor level.

cards.heading: A stain on the ceiling below
cards.body: On a second-floor bathroom, a rounded brown or gray stain on the ceiling underneath, or a small sag in the drywall, often traces back to the pan or the drain connection. If the stain grows after a shower and not after a toilet flush or a laundry cycle, that timing is useful information.

cards.heading: A musty smell you cannot clean away
cards.body: A persistent earthy or damp-basement odor in a bathroom that you scrub regularly usually means wet organic material somewhere you cannot reach: paper facing on drywall, the plywood or particleboard subfloor, or framing. Bleach on the surface does nothing for it because the source is behind the surface.

cards.heading: Efflorescence or a chalky white bloom
cards.body: White powdery deposits along grout lines or at the base of the shower curb mean water is moving through cementitious material, dissolving minerals, and depositing them as it evaporates. It is direct evidence of ongoing water travel, not just splash.

sections.heading: What the water is doing while you are still deciding it is nothing
sections.body:
Water leaving a failed pan does not pour. It wicks. It moves along the path of least resistance, and in a typical bathroom that path is the mortar bed, then the subfloor, then the sill plate and the bottom of the studs.

In the first stage, the mortar bed stays permanently saturated. It never dries between showers, so it loses compressive strength and starts to crumble, which is what makes tiles sound hollow and eventually crack. In the second stage, the water reaches the substrate: plywood or OSB subfloor delaminates and swells, particleboard turns to mush, and in a slab-on-grade home common across the Phoenix area the water spreads laterally between the slab and the flooring, which is why the first visible damage is often a doorway or a hall closet several feet away. In the third stage it reaches framing and drywall. Bottom plates stay wet, drywall wicks moisture upward from the floor, and microbial growth begins on the paper facing, usually on the hidden side first. Given enough time, fasteners corrode and the tile assembly loses the mechanical connection holding it together.

One more thing worth knowing about the desert: low indoor humidity makes surfaces dry fast, so the visible clues disappear between uses while the buried material stays wet. A homeowner here can genuinely believe the problem resolved itself for months while the subfloor never dries at all.

sections.heading: Simple checks that separate a pan leak from something else
sections.body: Before assuming the worst, it helps to rule out the cheaper explanations. Splash escaping past a short shower door sweep, a leaking supply valve inside the wall, a bad tub spout diverter, or a failed drain gasket can all mimic pan failure. The standard test is a flood test. Plug the shower drain with a test plug or an inflatable ball, fill the pan with water up to just below the curb, mark the water line with tape, and leave it for 24 hours. If the level drops noticeably or moisture appears below or beside the shower with no water running, the pan or the drain assembly is losing water. If the level holds and you still get damage only when someone showers, suspect the walls, the door, or the plumbing behind the valve instead. Do not run this test if you already see active water in a ceiling below, or if the finished space underneath cannot tolerate more water. A moisture meter pressed against the baseboard behind the shower, compared to a reading from the same baseboard across the room, will also tell you quickly whether that dark patch is old staining or currently wet material. When the answer turns out to be a wet subfloor or wet framing, the work splits into two parts: drying and removing the compromised material, which is water damage restoration, and then rebuilding the shower assembly, subfloor, and finishes, which is reconstruction and rebuild. Knowing which one you are looking at, or that you are looking at both, is usually the thing that finally makes the problem feel manageable.

faqs.q: Can a shower pan be repaired, or does the whole shower have to come out?
faqs.a: It depends on where the failure is. A loose drain clamp, a cracked drain body, or clogged weep holes can sometimes be addressed by removing only the shower floor tile and the mortar around the drain. A membrane that has split at a fold or was never turned up the walls correctly generally cannot be patched reliably in place, because the failure point is under tile and behind the bottom course of wall tile. Anyone who inspects it should be able to show you which of the two you have before quoting the work.

faqs.q: How long does it take for a leaking shower pan to cause real damage?
faqs.a: There is no fixed timeline, because it depends on how much water escapes per shower, how often the shower is used, and what material is underneath. What is consistent is the pattern: the material closest to the leak stays wet continuously, and continuously wet wood, mortar, and drywall lose strength and support microbial growth. The damage is usually well underway by the time it becomes visible in an adjacent room.

faqs.q: Why does the damage show up in the hallway instead of the bathroom?
faqs.a: Water follows the path of least resistance and the slope of the substrate, not the shape of the room. Tile and a sealed shower floor hold water in place; the seam where the bathroom flooring meets the hallway, or the gap along a wall plate, gives it somewhere to surface. On a slab foundation especially, water can travel several feet before it appears at an edge or a transition strip.

faqs.q: Does homeowners insurance cover a shower pan leak?
faqs.a: Coverage varies by policy and carrier, and it often turns on whether the loss is treated as sudden and accidental or as long-term seepage. Policies also commonly distinguish between the cost of fixing the failed component itself and the cost of repairing the resulting damage. Document what you see with dated photos, note when you first noticed it, and ask your carrier directly rather than assuming either way.
